title: Now let me go in peace (Luke 2:21–35)
hookLine: Simeon holds the child and says he can die content; Mary is told a sword will pierce her soul

lines: FORTY DAYS, UP TO THE TEMPLE.
TWO BIRDS: A POOR FAMILY'S OFFERING.
ONE MAN WALKS STRAIGHT TOWARD THEM.
cards: Forty days after the birth, Joseph and Mary carry the baby up to the temple in Jerusalem, to do what the law of Moses asked of new parents. Luke tells us their offering: a pair of turtledoves, or two young pigeons.
The law allowed birds instead of a lamb for families who couldn't afford one. So this is a poor couple with a newborn, in the crowded temple courts. Nobody pays them attention.
Except one man, who has waited a long time for this exact moment, and walks straight toward them.

teach.b: His name is Simeon. In the King James Bible, he was "just and devout, waiting for the consolation of Israel: and the Holy Ghost was upon him."
It had been revealed to him that he would not die before he saw the Lord's Christ.
He takes the baby in his arms and sings: "Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word: For mine eyes have seen thy salvation."
In Latin it begins Nunc dimittis, now you dismiss.
The Greek verb is the one used for releasing a servant from duty, or relieving a watchman at the end of his shift. Simeon has stood watch his whole life. Now he's off duty.
He calls the child "A light to lighten the Gentiles, and the glory of thy people Israel." Both: the nations and his own people. A surprise: Luke never says Simeon was old.
People assume it because he's ready to die, and artists have always painted him with a white beard. The text just says he was waiting. Then he turns to Mary, and the song changes key.
This child will cause the fall and rising of many, a sign that people will speak against, and: "Yea, a sword shall pierce through thy own soul also."

teach.h: NOW LETTEST THOU THY SERVANT DEPART IN PEACE.
teach.b: A warning in the middle of the blessing. Christians have long heard in it the cross, and Mary standing near it. Catholic devotion remembers this as the first of Mary's sorrows.
Joy and grief in one embrace, over a poor family's child.

how: Christians in many traditions say or sing the Nunc Dimittis at the end of the day, at Compline or Evensong, and many churches keep February 2 as the Presentation of the Lord, also called Candlemas.

games.why: "Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word: for mine eyes have seen thy salvation."

practice: Look back over today and name one good thing your eyes saw: a face, a kindness, a moment of light, even a small one.
Then notice what you're still standing watch over, and imagine setting it down for the night, like a watchman going off duty.
If you pray, you can say Simeon's words tonight, Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace; if not, let the day be finished, and rest.

wordCard.voice: Nunc dimittis. Latin for now you dismiss: Simeon's song, holding the child, ready to go in peace because his eyes have seen.

orig.note: Greek: you release, you dismiss. used for setting a servant free or relieving a watchman. in Latin, dimittis.

carryVoice: Your line: depart in peace. Even a watchman gets to go off duty. Day five hundred ten, done.
